item.title: The Thirteenth Mile: This Is What Gray Zone War Looks Like
item.description:
On the morning of October 23, the cargo ship Khoryv sent a distress call 13 nautical miles off Constanța, Romania. Territorial waters end at twelve. Whoever flew the drone that sank her knew where the line was, and chose to stand one mile outside it.

That mile is the story. It is the difference between an attack on a NATO member and an incident in a NATO member's exclusive economic zone. It is the difference between Article 5 and a press release. The London insurance market understood this before most capitals did. When the Joint War Committee extended its Black Sea listed area on September 16, it covered the entire sea except the territorial waters of Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey. The underwriters drew the same line the drone operators did. Nobody should find that comforting.

This is what gray zone conflict looks like. Freighters burning off the coasts of two NATO allies, sailors lost in cold water, and attacks clustered around the Sulina Channel, which became the main outlet for Ukrainian grain after Russia hammered Ukraine's own ports. It is war at a time and place of the attacker's choosing, priced just below the point where anyone is obliged to do anything about it.

"The problem is that we cannot prove it"

Bulgaria's prime minister, Rumen Radev, is nobody's idea of a Russia hawk. He told his parliament the logic of the attacks points to Moscow, and then said the quiet part out loud: "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

NATO's response has been built to solve Radev's problem. After the North Atlantic Council met on October 20, the Alliance announced it would send maritime patrol aircraft, radar, drones, intelligence personnel and forensic teams to examine the explosives. A U.S. Navy P-8 Poseidon is already flying the Black Sea. These are sensible deployments. They are also answers to the wrong question.

Play the scenario out. Grant NATO perfect attribution. The forensic teams recover a guidance board with Russian markings. The P-8 tracks a launch back to a known site. The Alliance announces, with high confidence, that the Russian Federation sank the ship. Now make it worse: the next drone hits a tanker alongside the pier at Constanța, the fire spreads, and thousands of civilians are dead.

The Kremlin denies it. Within the hour, Russian state media points at Kyiv, and it doesn't have to work hard to sell the story. Ukraine has been running its own maritime drone campaign since July, so the Black Sea is full of Ukrainian drones, and everyone knows it. A few Western commentators find the denial "plausible enough to warrant caution." Allies invoke Article 4 and consult. Statements are issued. Sanctions, already near their ceiling, are tightened at the margins. Then nothing happens, because every capital in the room is doing the same arithmetic: Russia has nuclear weapons, the Black Sea is not worth a war, and the dead are already dead.

You don't have to imagine that sequence. We ran it on July 17, 2014, when a Buk missile destroyed Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over eastern Ukraine and killed everyone aboard. A Dutch-led investigation established in 2016 that the launcher had been delivered from Russia, and by 2018 that it came from a Russian army unit. The ICAO Council found Russia responsible in May 2025. The European Court of Human Rights did the same that July. Moscow denied all of it, spent years promoting theories that blamed Ukraine, and in 2022 invaded the country the missile had been fired over. Attribution was as good as attribution gets. The consequence, eleven years later, was an order to enter into good-faith negotiations on reparations.

That is the lesson Moscow took from MH17, and it is the one we refuse to learn. Deniability is not a shield for the attacker. It is a gift to the defender who would rather not act. Russia doesn't need us to believe its denials. It only needs us to want to.

Operational freedom is the target

The point of these strikes isn't the ships. It's the water around them. Every hull that burns off Sulina raises the premium on the next one, pushes a charterer toward a different route, and teaches a shipowner that a NATO coastline offers no protection. The attacker never has to declare a blockade. The market imposes it for him. Freedom of action shrinks by increments, each too small to justify a response, until the defender wakes up to find that the sea he was sure he controlled has a new landlord.

This is how Russia and China will impose costs on the West for the foreseeable future. Not with the decisive battle our doctrine, our budgets, and our military exercises are built around, but with a steady accumulation of incidents chosen for their deniability, timed to our distractions, and calibrated to our fear of escalation. Salami slicing is not a new idea; Beijing has practiced it in the South China Sea for more than a decade. What's new is the drone, which makes the slicing cheap, precise and anonymous.

The honest complication

The Black Sea gray zone is not one-sided, and pretending otherwise hands Moscow its talking points. Ukraine's Operation Molochka, launched in July, claims to have disabled 300 Russian-linked vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. Turkey's foreign minister says both sides are mounting heavy attacks to establish superiority before winter.

The distinction holds. Ukraine is striking the logistics of the country that invaded it, mostly sanctioned tankers serving Russian ports and occupied Crimea. Russia is striking grain ships in the economic zones of two NATO members that are not party to the war, with the apparent aim of making Ukraine's last reliable export route uninsurable. One is a belligerent waging war at sea. The other is exporting that war to the Alliance's doorstep and daring it to notice.

Taiwan won't look like Hellscape

If you want to know what a Taiwan conflict will look like, watch the Black Sea.

In 2024, Adm. Samuel Paparo said he wanted to "turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape" to defeat what he described as Beijing's likely plan: a massive attack with little warning. It's a sound concept, and the CNAS work that fleshed it out this year is serious. Hellscape is built to break an amphibious assault at the water's edge.

Beijing is rehearsing something else. The PLA's Justice Mission 2025 drills in December, run alongside the China Coast Guard, simulated a blockade of Taiwan's main ports and control of the waterways that carry its energy imports. This year the China Coast Guard and Maritime Safety Administration have run what the Jamestown Foundation calls a "quasi-quarantine" east of the island, creating the appearance of administrative control without declaring a blockade. Taiwan has already prosecuted a Chinese captain for severing an undersea cable. Each step is a law enforcement action, an inspection, an accident. None of them is an invasion.

A drone swarm waiting in the Strait for a landing force has nothing to shoot at when the adversary is a coast guard cutter boarding a container ship for a "safety inspection." The first Taiwanese or American drone to fire makes Taipei the aggressor. So Beijing won't cross the Strait. It will tighten the noose: a quarantine, a severed cable, an insurance listing, a shipping line that quietly decides Kaohsiung isn't worth the premium. It will bank on the world's risk aversion. It’s already working. After the May summit in Beijing, Washington paused a record $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, and the President described those sales as a "very good negotiating chip". Taiwan will not be conquered. It will be persuaded, one closed option at a time, that there is nothing left to defend.

Answering below the threshold

You cannot deter gray zone coercion with a capability designed for the war the adversary is careful never to start. The answer has to live in the same band the attacker does: below the threshold of general war, above the threshold of pain. Three steps would help in the Black Sea, and each has a Pacific twin.

Presence that denies, not presence that watches. Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria already run a Mine Countermeasures Task Group whose mandate was widened in July to cover undersea infrastructure. Montreux restricts warships of non-Black Sea states, not the littoral navies. Widen the mandate once more, to counter-drone escort of merchant traffic through allied economic zones, and buy the equipment from the Ukrainians who have kept their own grain corridor open under fire. In the Pacific, the equivalent is a convoy and escort plan for a quarantine, not only a kill chain for an invasion.

Decide the response before the incident. The moment of decision is where risk aversion wins, because it is always easier to wait for one more forensic report. Allies should agree in advance, and say publicly, what a verified strike on shipping in their waters will cost Moscow: a pre-approved tranche of capability released to Ukraine, a pre-agreed number of shadow fleet hulls detained. Attribution should trigger an equivalent consequence, not another discussion. Taipei and Washington need the same menu for a quarantine, written now, while no one is under pressure.

Take the market off the adversary's side. When insurers and charterers do the attacker's work, governments need a sovereign war-risk backstop for vessels trading to allied ports, so the next listed-area extension doesn't function as a blockade by spreadsheet. Taiwan will need that backstop on the first day of a quarantine, not the ninetieth.

None of this is escalation. It is the minimum required to make the gray zone cost something.

The Thirteenth Mile

The Khoryv went down one mile outside a line we drew. The adversary picked the mile. Next time it will pick the hour, the cargo, the flag and the ocean. The question for the Alliance isn't whether we can prove who did it. It's whether, once we prove it, we will do anything.

item.title: The Intelligence Community’s Missing Discipline
item.description:
Economic statecraft has become a primary instrument of US national security, deployed with a frequency and ambition that outpaces the intelligence architecture built to support it. For sanctions, tariffs, investment screening, export controls, and development finance to succeed, the United States must fully leverage the data and intelligence available to it. Now is the time for the IC to organize itself around the discipline of economic and financial intelligence.

The IC has long struggled to prove its value to economic customers: the Secretaries of Treasury, Commerce, Defense, and State, as well as the US Trade Representative and financial regulators. One frequent explanation is the IC’s historic orientation toward military and diplomatic support. Another is the perception that classified economic analysis lacks distinctive value. I spent most of a twenty-three-year intelligence career inside the economic discipline, ultimately leading Treasury’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis (OIA). While this may once have been true, the IC is doing better than ever to meet growing demand.

The problem is no longer the quality of the analysis—which has matured immensely—but the IC’s decentralized approach to serving its economic customers. No IC agency is specifically responsible for the discipline of economic and financial intelligence. The closest is OIA.

Congress created OIA in statute in 2004 with an eye toward sanctions support and countering terrorism finance. Its role has since expanded across economic, financial, and cyber issues for customers across government and industry. However, OIA is not the designated IC lead for US economic statecraft—no IC agency is. One consequence is that the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) remains the statutory lead for analytic support to the Treasury-led Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). That made sense in 2007, when the Foreign Investment and National Security Act codified CFIUS and assigned the Director of National Intelligence that role. At the time, OIA was in its infancy and consumed by counterterrorism. That is no longer the case.

The instinct in Washington is to solve a challenge like this by first creating a new organization, then fixing the functions. Congress should start with the functions instead, then address where the discipline sits. To improve IC support to economic statecraft, Congress must first act on six fronts.

Designate a functional manager. One IC element must own economic and financial intelligence as a discipline: collection priorities, analytic standards, a hiring and training pipeline, and a framework for systematic engagement with allies and industry. Nothing about that role requires a new agency.

Clarify authorities. Explicitly authorize collaboration between the designated lead and both its government customers and the private sector, including exchange of expertise and data.

Supercharge private sector engagement. Many of the best national security solutions in economics and finance will come from industry. Create a permanent path for its ideas, expertise, and capabilities.

Work with what exists. Use OIA as the foundation and keep the number of IC agencies flat, but cap its size so it stays nimble as economic statecraft evolves.

Revisit ODNI’s CFIUS role. IC support to CFIUS sits with ODNI because in 2007 no one else could carry it. Whether it should move depends on where the discipline lands, but Congress should not view the 2007 answer as permanent.

Fund it as a national mission. Economic intelligence should not have to compete for a share of a domestic department’s topline. Give the discipline a dedicated budget line, with the investment in people and AI that exploiting economic data at scale requires.

That leaves where the discipline sits—and there are three answers, not one.

The easiest first step is a designation: name OIA the functional manager, leave it in Treasury, and make clear in statute and to policy customers that OIA is the center of gravity for economic and financial intelligence. That is available now and beats the status quo. Nevertheless, an IC office answering to the Secretary of the Treasury will always be seen—correctly—as Treasury’s first. This is why Commerce and others periodically press for shops of their own, an outcome that grows the IC rather than optimizing it.

The achievable reform is bureau status. Treasury did this with FinCEN in 2002, and FinCEN is now treated as a government-wide and international resource rather than Treasury’s alone. Done properly it means a separate appropriation, a director accountable to both the Secretary and the DNI, and a statutory mission naming service to the whole government, the private sector, and our allies.

The stretch option is to elevate OIA to become an independent National Geo-Economic Intelligence Agency—still my own preference, because only independence settles the question of whose intelligence office it is. But where the discipline sits is the last decision, not the first. Under any of the three, the proximity OIA has built with Treasury policymakers is a design problem with a known solution: dedicated, co-located teams at each major customer department.

Economic intelligence is a core national security capability and should be organized and resourced like one: purpose-built to track, anticipate, and disrupt adversary financial and commercial threats in real time. The playbook has changed. Our competitors are more agile, emboldened, and shaping markets and supply chains to their advantage while we debate whether the threat qualifies as strategic.

item.title: We’re Losing the Cognitive Space Race
item.description:
Over the last century, modern medicine achieved a historic feat. We increased the human lifespan by 33%. But at the same time, we completely failed to defend our brain healthspan. Today, a silent gap of 15 to 30 years exists between the time our bodies survive and the time our brains remain vibrant, innovative, and fully functional. It is a terrifying paradox. Medical science has advanced so much that a newborn today can realistically expect to live to 100, if not 120 years old. Yet, we passively accept that their cognitive engine will begin an irreversible, downhill slide in their thirties with the likelihood of dementia reaching almost 100% by the age of 110. What good is an extra three decades of biological existence if our brains lack the strength and resilience to enjoy it? This is no longer just a localized healthcare crisis; it is an imminent national security threat to our competitive edge.

Look at where our national focus and funding are directed. America is focused on investing billions of dollars into artificial intelligence and hypersonic defense systems. However, we are systematically ignoring the ultimate computing engine that builds the technology, commands our military, drives our economy, and stabilizes our communities: the human brain.

Our global competitors are not making this mistake. Most notably, China understands that future geopolitical dominance will not be won simply by hoarding raw technology. It will be won by the cognitive longevity, relentless innovation, and emotional resilience of their population. They are playing the long game and investing in their brain economy; We are falling behind.

In the military, we use a concept called staying "left of boom." It means executing proactive, aggressive conditioning and preventative strategies to stop a catastrophe before it happens, rather than digging through the wreckage after an explosion.

Right now, America’s approach to brain health is reactive. Our public policy treats brain aging as an inevitable, downhill slide into deficit. We pour billions of dollars into solving brain health collapse, like dementia and visible cognitive breakdown, before we actively intervene. But that approach is a losing strategy. We must shift from a reactive, disease-focused model to a proactive era of precision brain health in order to finally maximize American brainpower. If we do not actively optimize our collective intelligence and mental endurance, we will fall behind not only in defense readiness but also in scientific advancement and workforce productivity.

Fortunately, building a sharper, more resilient nation has never been easier or more measurable.

A landmark, three-year longitudinal study of 4,000 adults recently published in Nature Portfolio’s Scientific Reports completely dismantles the myth of inevitable cognitive decline. The data proves that the human brain possesses a no-ceiling capability. From ages 19 to 94, the brain retains a profound capacity to continually rewire, adapt, and improve its performance over time.

The key to unlocking this potential is a newly validated, multidimensional metric called the BrainHealth Index. For the first time, we can treat the brain exactly like physical fitness. We don't guess if our hearts are healthy; we measure blood pressure. The BrainHealth Index finally gives us a credible benchmark to track and measure holistic brain improvement across three critical pillars:

  • Clarity: Our raw capacity to solve complex, novel problems and drive deep technological innovation.
  • Connectedness: Our capacity for social purpose and communication, which serves as the bedrock for stable families and strong communities.
  • Emotional Balance: The mental resilience required to perform under extreme pressure, from corporate boardrooms to tactical defense environments.

When we actively invest in and train our cognitive micro-skills, the positive implications ripple across society. Every day, citizens become better in their personal relationships, more productive at their jobs, and significantly more resilient against modern burnout and life stressors. Scaled nationally, this collective mental fitness becomes the invisible armor required for our national defense and technological endurance.

As a neurologist, a retired U.S. Army Colonel, and the former founding director of DARPA’s Biological Technologies Office, I have spent my entire career protecting and restoring the brains of our service members. I know what the human mind is capable of achieving when it is pushed to optimize, rather than just manage decline.

Our federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services, the NIH, and the Department of Veterans Affairs, must immediately work to adopt scalable, digital health initiatives that democratize these brain optimization tools nationwide. But executive action is only half the battle. Congress must step up and introduce a unified, bipartisan National Brain Capital Act. Just as lawmakers realized we could not secure our future without a CHIPS and Science Act to defend our artificial intelligence hardware, they must recognize that we cannot protect our nation without a legislative framework to maximize our human brainpower. We must empower every single citizen with the self-agency to improve their own cognitive capacity. It is time for Congress to stop treating brain performance as a passive medical luxury for the few. It is a national imperative to keep America leading the world.

item.title: How Houthi attacks have grounded flights across Saudi Arabia
item.description:

item.title: Starc takes six as Australia fight back in South Africa decider
item.description:
Mitchell Starc said a “reset at lunch” led to an Australian fightback after South Africa made a flying start on the first day of the third Test at Newlands on Tuesday.

Starc finished with six for 72 as South Africa were bowled out for 329 shortly before the close in a match which will decide a series between the two leading Test nations.

It was a performance which looked unlikely as South Africa raced to 140 without loss at lunch after being sent in.

Starc was one of the bowlers punished, with the tall left-arm pacer conceding 39 runs in seven overs, including four successive boundaries by Marques Ackerman, who went on to score a rapid 95.

“We probably expected more out of the wicket,” said Starc. “It was quite slow, with tennis ball bounce. They came at us hard.

“We didn’t have our best stuff in the first two hours but the last two sessions were right up there. It’s what we expect from this group. We had a reset at lunch and just tried to change the momentum in the field.”

Ackerman, playing in his second Test, took the fight to the Australian bowlers with some dazzling strokes.

The slightly-built left-hander was on 82 not out at lunch, scored off just 75 balls.

He attacked veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon, dancing down the pitch and hitting him over the stand at midwicket for six. But he tried one shot too many after lunch and was stranded when Lyon pushed the ball wider, giving Alex Carey an easy stumping.

Ackerman, 30, said South Africa would probably have been happy if they had been offered a total of 329 before play.

But he admitted: “We probably left a few runs out there.”

Ackerman, who won a place in the side through strong domestic performances and some big scores for South Africa A, including 256 against Bangladesh A in August, is not normally an opening batsman but said he was not troubled by the adjustment.

“I have quite often had to face a new ball in my career and playing against our own fast bowlers in the nets has been good preparation,” he said.

item.title: Pakistan name U-19 squad for Asia Cup title defence
item.description:
Defending champions Pakistan on Tuesday announced a 15-member squad for the U-19 Asia Cup, which will be held in Oman from Nov 5 to 14.

Farhan Yousuf will lead the side, which is scheduled to depart for Oman from Karachi on Oct 29, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) said in a statement.

Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘A’ alongside India, Nepal and hosts the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the eight-team tournament.

The squad includes wicket-keeper-batters Abdul Qadir and Hamza Zahoor, and batters Usman Khan, Hayam Khan, Jahangir Bilal and Huzaifa Ahsan. All-rounders Ahmed Hussain and Hasnain Abbas Dar have also been included.

The pace attack comprises Abdul Subhan, Mohammad Seyam, Ali Raza and Rizwanullah, while Mohammad Huzaifa and Niqab Shafiq are the two frontline spin options.

Of the 15 players selected for the continental event, only Ali Raza and Huzaifa Ahsan were not part of the Pakistan U-19 side that defeated England 3-1 in a four-match Youth ODI series in September.

Pakistan won the previous edition of the tournament in the United Arab Emirates, defeating arch-rivals India by 191 runs in a one-sided final at the ICC Academy Ground in Dubai.

The team will begin their title defence against the UAE on Nov 6 before taking on India on Nov 8 and Nepal on Nov 10.

Group ‘B’ comprises Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Malaysia.

The semi-finals will be played on Nov 12, with the final scheduled for Nov 14.

Shahid Anwar will serve as head coach and team manager, while Rao Iftikhar Anjum has been named fast bowling coach and Zohaib Khan spin bowling coach. Humayun Farhat will be the fielding coach.

Squad: Farhan Yousuf (captain), Abdul Qadir (wicket-keeper), Abdul Subhan, Ahmed Hussain, Ali Raza, Hamza Zahoor (wicket-keeper), Hasnain Abbas Dar, Hayam Khan, Huzaifa Ahsan, Jahangir Bilal, Mohammad Huzaifa, Mohammad Seyam, Niqab Shafiq, Rizwanullah, Usman Khan.

item.title: Muneeba to lead Pakistan in Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy
item.description:
Muneeba Ali will captain Pakistan in the ICC Women’s Emerging Nations Trophy 2026, with the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Tuesday announcing a 14-member squad for the tournament to be held in Ajman, United Arab Emirates, from Nov 12 to 25.

Batter Ayesha Zafar has been appointed vice-captain of the side, which will feature 12 players retained from Pakistan’s previous assignment. Sadaf Shamas and Waheeda Akhtar have been recalled to the squad.

Regular captain Fatima Sana will miss the tournament as she prepares to feature in her maiden Women’s Big Bash League season in Australia.

The squad announcement comes after Pakistan secured a bronze medal at the Asian Games in Japan. Wicket-keeper-batter Gull Feroza, who was named the best wicketkeeper-batter at the recently concluded National Women’s T20 Tournament, has also been included.

The batting line-up comprises Ayesha, Eman Naseer, Eyman Fatima, Sadaf, Saira Jabeen and Shawaal Zulfiqar, while Muneeba and Gull provide wicket-keeping options.

Left-arm spinner Nashra Sundhu will spearhead the bowling attack, with Momina Riasat, Tuba Hassan and Umm-e-Hani completing the spin contingent. Tasmia Rubab and Waheeda are the two frontline pace options.

The 30-match tournament will feature 10 teams divided into two groups. Pakistan have been placed in Group B alongside Bangladesh, Thailand, the Netherlands and Zimbabwe.

Group ‘A’ comprises Sri Lanka, Ireland, Scotland, Papua New Guinea and hosts the United Arab Emirates.

The teams will first compete in a single-league round-robin stage, after which the top three sides from each group will advance to the Super Six stage. Each qualifying team will play three matches in that phase, with the top two progressing to the final on Nov 25.

The Pakistan squad will assemble in Lahore on Nov 6 and attend a pre-tournament training camp on Nov 7, 8 and 9 before departing for the UAE.

Squad: Muneeba Ali Siddiqui (captain, wicketkeeper), Ayesha Zafar (vice-captain), Eman Naseer, Eyman Fatima, Gull Feroza (wicket-keeper), Momina Riasat, Nashra Sundhu, Sadaf Shamas, Saira Jabeen, Shawaal Zulfiqar, Tasmia Rubab, Tuba Hassan, Umm-e-Hani and Waheeda Akhtar.

item.title: Prime Minister arrives in Tokyo on 4-day official visit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived in Tokyo Monday morning (local time) on a four-day official visit at the invitation of his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, aiming to deepen bilateral ties, attract investment and expand trade and development cooperation.

A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Zubaida Rahman, and members of his entourage landed at Narita International Airport at 9:07 am local time. 

The prime minister was received at the airport by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone. A motorcade then escorted him to Tokyo’s Imperial Hotel, where he will stay during his visit.

Japan to invest Tk 774.7 billion in Bangladesh

Prime Minister’s Adviser for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Foreign Employment in the Asia-Pacific region Md Shakirul Islam Khan, and senior officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo were also present.

Earlier, the prime minister left Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka early today Bangladesh time for Japan aboard a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight, accompanied by a small delegation.

Tarique Rahman is scheduled to hold a high-level bilateral talk with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at her office on 27 October, followed by a joint press announcement and a luncheon hosted by the Japanese premier, according to the Prime Minister’s press wing.

During the four-day visit, the prime minister will also meet Japanese government officials, development institutions and business leaders, visit industrial and energy facilities, and deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum.

The premier's visit is expected to deepen the existing strategic partnership, attract fresh Japanese investment, expand trade and accelerate ongoing development projects, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam told journalists at a curtain-raiser media briefing at the Foreign Ministry on 20 October.

Discussions will focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement.

What Bangladesh can gain from PM's Japan visit

The two sides will also explore wider cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development.

His tentative programme includes engagements with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation.

Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation, said the foreign secretary.

The proposed itinerary includes visits to an LNG terminal and power plant in Futtsu City, Chiba, the headquarters of UNIQLO and a Toyota factory in Nagoya.

The foreign secretary said the two sides were discussing draft memoranda of understanding and cooperation agreements covering agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernisation.

"We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit," he said.

Around eight MoUs are under discussion, of which three to four could be signed during the visit. Separate agreements are also being pursued in education and human resource development.

Detailed discussions are planned on Japanese support for establishing factories in Bangladesh, generating employment and developing human resources in line with the prime minister's priorities.

PM’s Japan visit: Reducing metro rail costs, loan interest rates likely to be discussed

The two sides are also expected to discuss regional and international peace and stability, a sustainable and peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis, stronger cooperation in addressing the energy crisis and efforts to end international conflicts.

The visit follows the prime minister's participation in an online meeting in April at the invitation of the Japanese premier, during which Bangladesh welcomed a Japan-led initiative to address energy challenges across Asia.

Japan has been a major development partner of Bangladesh since the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1972. Japanese assistance has supported major infrastructure projects, including the Dhaka metro rail, the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and infrastructure development in Matarbari.

item.title: Bangladesh retains top denim exporter to Europe; China, India, Vietnam are also ahead
item.description:
Bangladesh has retained its leading position in denim garment exports to the European Union (EU). However, the country’s denim exports declined in the first eight months of this year (January–August), while exports from competitors such as China, Egypt, Vietnam and India grew rapidly.

According to data from Eurostat, the EU’s statistical office, EU member states imported denim garments worth 2.95 billion euros from countries around the world in the first eight months of this year. This represented a 4.40 per cent decline compared with the same period last year.

Bangladesh’s denim exports to the EU fell more sharply than the bloc’s overall imports.

The country exported denim garments worth 870 million euros in the first eight months of this year, down 5.85 per cent from the same period last year. Bangladesh now accounts for 29.40 per cent of the EU denim garment market.

Pakistan ranks second among denim garment exporters to the EU. The country exported denim worth 530 million euros in the first eight months of this year, a decline of 7.88 per cent compared with the same period last year. Pakistan currently holds a 17.78 per cent share of the EU denim garment market.

Türkiye and Tunisia rank third and fourth, respectively, among denim garment exporters to the EU. Türkiye’s denim garment exports fell by 21 per cent in the first eight months of this year, reaching 440 million euros.

Meanwhile, Tunisia, in Africa, exported denim worth 220 million euros. This represented a 6.44 per cent decline compared with the same period last year.

Competing countries are gaining ground

The figures for the three countries immediately behind Bangladesh in the EU denim export market do not tell the whole story. Four competing countries are rapidly increasing their denim garment exports.

For example, while Bangladesh’s exports fell by nearly 6 per cent in the first eight months of this year, Vietnam’s rose by 45 per cent.

According to Eurostat data, China’s denim garment exports to the EU rose by 17.70 per cent year on year in the first eight months of this year, reaching 200 million euros. China now accounts for 6.67 per cent of the market.

Similarly, Egypt’s denim garment exports to the EU increased by 31.46 per cent to 200 million euros between January and August. Egypt also holds a 6.67 per cent share of the market.

Cambodia and Morocco, which follow in the rankings, recorded declines of 6.47 per cent and 14.48 per cent, respectively, in their denim garment exports. During the first eight months of this year, Cambodia exported denim worth 140 million euros, while Morocco’s exports amounted to 60 million euros.

Meanwhile, Vietnam exported denim garments worth 50 million euros to the EU in the first eight months of this year, a 45 per cent increase compared with the same period last year.

India also exported denim garments worth 30 million dollars between January and August, recording growth of 18.62 per cent.

Bangladesh’s denim exports recover in August

Although Bangladesh lagged behind in the EU market earlier this year, its denim garment exports rose by 12.71 per cent in August, reaching 134.1 million euros. Overall EU imports of denim garments also increased during the month, rising by 11.23 per cent to 4.3 billion euros.

Pakistan recorded faster export growth than Bangladesh. Its denim exports rose by nearly 15 per cent in August to 87.7 million euros. During the same period, Türkiye’s exports fell by 13 per cent, while Tunisia’s increased by around 5.5 per cent.

Meanwhile, China’s denim exports grew by around 17.5 per cent in August. Egypt recorded an increase of 59.5 per cent. Cambodia’s exports rose by nearly 11 per cent, while Vietnam’s surged by 56 per cent. India’s exports increased by 52 per cent.

Mohiuddin Rubel, a former director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and additional managing director (AMD) of Bangladesh Denim Experts, told Prothom Alo: “Although orders remained low during the first five months of the year, the following three months were somewhat better. As a result, the rate of export decline is slowing. However, competing countries have recorded higher export growth than us. One of the main reasons is that we cannot offer buyers competitive prices. Factories are struggling with high gas and electricity costs, as well as other challenges. This is pushing up production costs. Moreover, our product range is less diversified than that of our competitors.”

In response to another question, Mohiuddin Rubel said: “Vietnam has signed a free trade agreement (FTA) with the EU, while India is in the final stages of negotiating one. As a result, buyers are becoming increasingly interested in sourcing denim garments from these two countries. Once Bangladesh graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category, it will lose preferential market access under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) after a specified transition period. We must therefore take effective steps to negotiate FTAs as well to secure duty-free market access.”

item.title: Women constitute 63pc of medical students
item.description:
Female enrolment in medical education has risen significantly across Bangladesh. Women currently account for nearly 63 per cent of all students pursuing degrees in public and private medical colleges.

Female students also outnumber their male counterparts in dental education, while in nursing and midwifery programmes, women represent approximately 90 per cent of total enrolments.

However, the proportion of female physicians in the professional sphere, particularly in government jobs, remains comparatively lower.

The trend of advancement of women observed at the primary, secondary, and higher secondary levels is visibly mirrored in medical education.

Nevertheless, this continuity is not uniformly maintained across the university sector. Outside the affiliated colleges of the National University, the proportion of female students in public and private universities remains below 40 per cent.

The predominance of female students in medical colleges has been evident for the past eight to 10 years. The number of female graduates passing the MBBS examinations also exceeds that of males.

Consequently, female participation among newly qualifying physicians entering the workforce is expanding at a higher rate than previously recorded.

The report titled Bangladesh Education Statistics 2025, published by the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS), outlines the trajectory of women's progress in medical education alongside general education metrics.

In the 39th (Special) BCS examination, the Public Service Commission (PSC) recommended 6,792 physicians for appointment. Among those recommended, 53 per cent were male and 47 per cent female, despite women comprising over 56 per cent of the total applicant pool.

According to the report, in 2025, a total of 51,313 students were enrolled across 109 public and private medical colleges nationwide (with two additional colleges receiving approval subsequently). Of these students, 62.79 per cent were female. In the 37 public medical colleges, women comprised 61.57 per cent of the total student body. Meanwhile, in the 72 private medical colleges, the proportion of female students stood at 63.60 per cent.

Medical student crisis: No compromise with quality of education

Medical colleges impart training through the MBBS degree programme. The clear female majority in this course indicates that women now constitute a substantial proportion of those on the path to becoming medical professionals. The leading position of female students is evident across both public and private institutions.

However, in the professional workforce, specifically in the government jobs, female physicians continue to lag behind slightly. In the 39th (Special) BCS examination, the Public Service Commission (PSC) recommended 6,792 physicians for appointment. Among those recommended, 53 per cent were male and 47 per cent female, despite women comprising over 56 per cent of the total applicant pool.

A similar pattern emerged in the 42nd (Special) BCS examination, where 4,000 physicians were recommended for recruitment. Of these, approximately 51 per cent were male and 49 per cent female, while women accounted for nearly 56 per cent of the applicants.

Women lead in dentistry and nursing as well

Female representation is dominant not only in MBBS programmes but also across other health-related academic disciplines. According to Education Statistics 2025, nearly 7,500 students are currently enrolled across the country's 35 dental colleges and dental units, of whom 60.85 per cent are female.

Syed Abdul Hamid, Professor of the Institute of Health Economics at Dhaka UniversityFemale representation remains relatively low in several critical medical specialities as interest often remains concentrated in specific fields such as Obstetrics and Gynaecology.

Female participation is even higher in nursing and midwifery education. Bangladesh houses 475 nursing and midwifery colleges and institutes, with a combined student body of approximately 40,000. Nearly 90 per cent of them are female.

Physicians, dental surgeons, nurses, and midwives all play vital roles in forming a skilled healthcare workforce across various tiers of service delivery. However, sector experts note that alongside female numerical superiority in education, it is equally crucial to assess the extent to which their workforce participation, professional career progression, and leadership opportunities are advancing.

Women's advancement in Bangladesh vs. gender backlash

The trend of female predominance in medical education is not entirely new. Statistics from the Directorate General of Health Education (DGHE) on medical admissions and MBBS pass rates between 2009 and 2018 corroborate this pattern.

According to the data, a total of 48,777 domestic students cleared the MBBS examinations over that decade, of whom 26,901 were female, representing roughly 55 per cent of all successful graduates.

Academic merit, family encouragement, and educational progress

Education professionals attribute the growing representation of women in medical education to several major factors. Female participation has expanded at the primary, secondary, and higher secondary levels, where the proportion of female students currently exceeds 50 per cent.

Girls also outperform boys in achieving GPA-5, the highest performance benchmark in public examinations. As a result, female participation in the competitive admission exams for higher education continues to grow.

He stressed the importance of strategically encouraging broader female participation across diverse medical specialities to establish a balanced distribution, suggesting that the issue requires deliberation at the policy-making level.

At the same time, according to them, the strong interest of high-achieving female students in pursuing a medical career, alongside encouraging family support, plays a pivotal role. Socioeconomic background, access to education, career preferences, and success in admission examinations further contribute to this trend.

Another significant facet of female participation in medical education is their professional field of choice.

Researchers from the BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health and icddr,b (International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh) analysed data from 34,697 physicians registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (BMDC) between 2006 and 2015.

Women lag behind in higher education and employment

The analysis revealed that among registered physicians, 48 per cent were male and 52 per cent female. Notably, 87 per cent of male physicians with specialised qualifications were concentrated in Medicine and Surgery, whereas 96 per cent of female physicians with specialised qualifications held expertise in Obstetrics and Gynaecology.

This research paper was published in the online medical journal PLOS ONE in January 2019.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Professor Syed Abdul Hamid of the Institute of Health Economics at Dhaka University noted that the academic excellence and advancement of female students represent a positive development.

Academic records trapped in files: Our struggles in higher education

According to him, they secure admission to medical colleges on the basis of merit through highly competitive entrance examinations. However, certain barriers persist in the professional workplace.

Owing to working environments and logistical realities in rural and district-level areas, female physicians frequently encounter distinct challenges in performing their duties, he stated.

Professor Abdul Hamid pointed out that female representation remains relatively low in several critical medical specialities as interest often remains concentrated in specific fields such as Obstetrics and Gynaecology.

He stressed the importance of strategically encouraging broader female participation across diverse medical specialities to establish a balanced distribution, suggesting that the issue requires deliberation at the policy-making level.

item.title: Japan only major development partner to pledge new loans in three months
item.description:
Development partners such as the World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), China, Russia and India made no loan commitments during the first three months (July–September) of the current fiscal year.

Among the major development partners, only Japan committed to providing loans, pledging USD 3.5 million during the period. However, major development partners disbursed loans they had committed earlier.

The Economic Relations Division (ERD) released its latest report on the country's foreign loan situation for July–September, the first quarter of the fiscal year, on Monday. The report contains these findings.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is currently visiting Japan. During the visit, investment agreements worth approximately USD 14 billion are expected to be signed for the next five years.

The World Bank and the ADB led foreign loan disbursements in the current fiscal year. The World Bank disbursed the highest amount during the first three months (July–September), providing USD 196.5 million.

The ADB ranked second, disbursing USD 162.1 million during the period. India, in third place, provided USD 105 million. Russia disbursed USD 20 million, while China provided USD 15 million.

Loan disbursements halve

According to ERD figures, debt repayments have increased, with repayments now exceeding disbursements by more than twofold.

Development partners and countries disbursed approximately USD 660 million in loans during the first three months (July–September) of the current fiscal year, half the amount disbursed during the same period last year. In the first quarter of the previous fiscal year, loan disbursements amounted to USD 1.15 billion.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh had to repay approximately USD 1.35 billion in principal and interest on previously borrowed loans during the same period.

The country received loan commitments worth just USD 1.27 billion during July–September.

BGB personnel have been on duty in the constituency since Sunday, according to Thakurgaon Battalion (50 BGB).
The troops have been deployed across three upazilas, 22 unions and one municipality within the constituency. They will operate as mobile units and striking forces in their assigned areas.
Intelligence operations have also been intensified to strengthen security. At a press briefing, BGB officials said personnel were using body-worn cameras and drones to monitor key locations.
The force said its primary objective was to ensure that voters could cast their ballots safely and without obstruction.
Officials said BGB personnel are also monitoring the situation to ensure candidates have equal opportunities to campaign and that the electoral code of conduct is followed.
The force remains on alert to prevent unrest, violence and other activities that could threaten public safety during the election. Surveillance and patrols have also been strengthened in border areas.

Saudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks
item.description:
IRAN-CRISIS/SAUDI-TURKEY-PAKISTAN

Top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday in a bid to de-escalate the Middle East conflict, as Yemen's Houthis launched new attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt approved defence support for the Gulf kingdom.

The talks were the first high-level contact between Iran and the three nations — which signed the Mecca mutual defence pact in August — since a war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran also spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

The Saudi Foreign Ministry said the visit was intended to open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation".

Saudi Arabia was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, younger brother of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Pakistan by army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir; and Turkey by intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, Saudi and Iranian officials said.

Iranian state media published pictures of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, attending the meetings. At the conclusion of the meetings, the four states agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation, especially in peace and security, state media reported.

Pakistan and Qatar have led mediation efforts in the war. Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday, an official told Reuters.

Earlier efforts helped produce an interim peace agreement in June but fighting between Iran and the United States soon resumed. Conflict then flared between the Iran-aligned Houthis and US ally Saudi Arabia, opening a new front.

US and Iran threaten new attacks

The wider fighting has restricted shipping through the energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz, pushed up global oil and gas prices, left Gulf states facing missile and drone attacks, and caused a new humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

Tensions between Washington and Tehran have sharpened in recent days. President Donald Trump said on Friday the US may carry out another military operation against Iran. Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the United States and Israel attack again.

The war, which earlier in the year also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese Hezbollah militia, has eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the USmidterm elections that decide control of Congress.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday's discussions would include "Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and the repercussions of US and Israeli military action against Iran".

Baghaei said the meeting, proposed when Munir visited Tehran last week, could be a first step towards establishing regional security mechanisms. A senior Pakistani security official said the focus of Monday's meeting was to build a regional non-aggression network. The agenda also included US-Iran talks, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and a US blockade of Iranian ports, the official said.

Another Pakistani official said Munir, with a go-ahead from Trump to try diplomacy, had presented Iran with a solution to the conflict. The current proposal would offer something to both the US and Iran, the official said, without giving details. The Mecca pact states and Qatar could act as guarantors if it was accepted, the official added.

An Iranian official had earlier said there would be no discussion of Iran's nuclear programme at Monday's meeting and the issue would not be addressed until Tehran's demands for ending the war were met. Those conditions include ending a US blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports. US Vice President JD Vance has said Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war.

Pakistan's military media office and Turkey's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Parliament approves Egyptian defence support for Saudis

Saudi Arabia has ⁠intensified strikes against the Houthis since they captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing against Saudi-backed government forces. The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, ports and oil installations.

On Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as well as Riyadh airport, which said it had resumed operations at two terminals a day earlier. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the Houthi attacks.

The parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the Mecca pact, on Monday authorised the Egyptian military to help defend Saudi Arabia, a major financial and political partner for Cairo.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement says signatories shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

The pact's members held an emergency meeting in Riyadh this month and agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Efforts by Turkey’s parliament to ratify the agreement began last week and are still under way, while Pakistan approved the pact last week.

item.title: PM’s Japan visit to renew investment ties, recover lost opportunities: Humaiun
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Japan offers an opportunity to recover business and investment opportunities missed over the past 15 years and build a renewed bilateral partnership based on transparency, accountability and sustainable investment, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said today.

“A trust deficit and corruption had hindered bilateral relations and business opportunities under the previous Sheikh Hasina government, while the country’s democratic transition had opened the way for a renewed partnership with Japan,” he said at a press briefing at the Bangladesh Embassy here this evening marking the first day of Prime Minister's four-day visit to Japan.

The state minister said, “Through this democratic transition, we want to build a relationship with Japan that has transparency, accountability and a sustainable, promising investment partnership.”

“Bangladesh no longer wants to move forward through dependency. It will now stand on its own feet and become a partner on the basis of investment,” he added.

The state minister said the visit had generated international interest in Bangladesh following the democratic transition after the August 5 uprising and the formation of an elected government.

He said the country’s foreign and economic policies and the activities of the new government had attracted interest from stakeholders in different parts of the world. He also pointed to interest among Japanese government officials and private-sector representatives in engaging with Bangladesh and exploring investment opportunities.

Describing the visit as an important milestone in Bangladesh-Japan relations, Kobir recalled that Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman visited Japan in 1978 and 1980, while former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia visited the country in 1994 and 2005.

He said the current visit offered an opportunity to carry forward the historical relationship and identify new areas of cooperation.

On the first day of the four-day state visit, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held meetings with a high-level Japanese parliamentary delegation led by former Prime Minister Taro Aso, Marubeni Corporation Chairman Masumi Kakinoki and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) President Dr Akihiko Tanaka.

The discussions covered strengthening bilateral relations, expanding trade and Japanese investment, technology transfer, skills development and cooperation in infrastructure and other development priorities.

During the meeting with Aso, the Prime Minister recalled their meeting in Japan in 2006 and acknowledged Aso’s contribution to strengthening bilateral relations. He also invited Aso to visit Bangladesh again, Kobir said.

At the meeting with Kakinoki, discussions covered expanding trade and investment, implementing the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) signed in February, and Japanese investment in information and communication technology, energy and advanced manufacturing.

The Prime Minister also discussed modernising Karnaphuli Fertilizer Company Limited and exploring the possibility of establishing a second fertiliser factory.

During the meeting with JICA President Tanaka, the Prime Minister discussed continued Japanese support for infrastructure and economic development projects, faster implementation of ongoing projects, and proposals for a Bangladesh-Japan Skills Partnership and a Technological Village and Innovation City. Agricultural modernisation, agro-processing, light engineering and energy security were also discussed.

Kobir said the meetings demonstrated the scope for expanding economic cooperation and creating new investment opportunities in Bangladesh.
The day’s final engagement was a dinner hosted in the Prime Minister’s honour by Nippon Foundation Chairman Yohei Sasakawa.

The state minister said the visit would continue with further engagements over the next three days, including bilateral talks between Tarique Rahman and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi tomorrow.

“Through this visit, we want to build a relationship that is based on transparency, accountability and a sustainable investment partnership,” Kobir said, expressing hope that the engagement would help Bangladesh and Japan advance their relations on the basis of mutual interests.

Prime Minister’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon, Deputy Press Secretary Shahadat Shadhin, members of the Prime Minister’s Press Wing and senior officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo were present at the press briefing.

item.title: 15 senior officials, including 3 secretaries, to visit Türkiye to gain experience
item.description:
The government is sending 15 senior officials from various ministries and divisions, including three secretaries, on a visit to Türkiye. The aim is to gain experience and seek assistance from Türkiye in areas including defence, education, technology and disaster management. Scheduled for late next month, the visit will be funded by the Turkish government.

The Bangladesh delegation will be led by Shahriar Kader Siddiky, secretary of the Economic Relations Division (ERD). The other two secretaries are Munshi Alauddin Al Azad, secretary of the Ministry of Religious Affairs, and Mohammad Saiful Islam, secretary of the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief.

Officials from various offices and departments, including the Prime Minister’s Office and the ministries of public administration, defence, industries, science and technology, and commerce, as well as the Health Services Division and the Secondary and Higher Education Division, will also be part of the delegation.

An ERD order has confirmed the visit, stating that the Turkish government will bear all expenses for the Bangladesh delegation.

Officials concerned with the visit said delegation members could not recall whether such a large group of senior government officials had ever visited Türkiye together before. In the past, large groups of government officials have undertaken similar visits to several European countries, Japan and India.

Speaking to several officials named on the delegation list, Prothom Alo learned that the incumbent government is keen to take relations with Türkiye to a new level. Türkiye, too, is attaching considerable importance to its relationship with Bangladesh. Against this backdrop, the 15-member high-level delegation is visiting the country to expand cooperation in various fields, including defence, education, technology and disaster management.

The visit is scheduled for 23–27 November.

Exchanges of visits between the two countries increase

Relations between Bangladesh and Türkiye have experienced tensions in the past. During the ousted Awami League government, the execution of Jamaat-e-Islami's top leaders convicted in war crimes cases relating to crimes against humanity during the 1971 Liberation War created unease in bilateral relations. Türkiye's objections to the trials and executions affected diplomatic ties between the two countries.

Sources within the government said defence trade, investment, joint production and the Rohingya crisis were among the major issues discussed during the Turkish foreign minister's visit. Fidan also spoke of efforts to elevate relations between Bangladesh and Türkiye to a strategic level.

However, relations began to normalise towards the end of the Awami League government's tenure. Bilateral ties gained momentum during the interim government, and government sources say the trend has continued under the current BNP government.

A meeting of world leaders at COP31 is scheduled to take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 10 to 12 November. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected to visit Türkiye to attend the meeting.

Earlier this month, Shafiqur Rahman, leader of the opposition in parliament and ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, visited Türkiye. He took part in several programmes and held meetings with leaders at various levels.

Before that, Chief of Army Staff General Waker-Uz-Zaman undertook a five-day official visit to Türkiye in July.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Bangladesh on 5 and 6 June. During the visit, he held talks with his Bangladeshi counterpart and met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. At the meetings, Fidan expressed Türkiye's interest in deepening its long-standing partnership with Bangladesh and expanding cooperation across a broader range of areas.

Sources within the government said defence trade, investment, joint production and the Rohingya crisis were among the major issues discussed during the Turkish foreign minister's visit. Fidan also spoke of efforts to elevate relations between Bangladesh and Türkiye to a strategic level.

Bangladesh will seek assistance in transferring technology to university students, introducing artificial intelligence (AI) technology in educational institutions and establishing laboratories. The delegation will also discuss training programmes to improve the skills of Bangladeshi government officials.

In July, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam told journalists that a drone manufacturing plant would be established in Bogura with Turkish assistance. He said the factory would be located near the international airport planned for the district.

Against this backdrop, the latest visit by officials from various ministries is being viewed as an initiative to strengthen administrative and institutional ties between the two countries.

In 2022, Bangladesh's armed forces signed an agreement with a Turkish company to procure drones.

A meeting of the Bangladesh–Türkiye Joint Economic Commission (JEC) is scheduled to be held in Dhaka on 20 and 21 January next year.

Government sources said the November visit by the 15-member Bangladeshi delegation could help identify areas for cooperation and facilitate discussions. Several agreements or memorandums of understanding may subsequently be signed at the JEC meeting.

Cooperation in defence, Rohingya affairs and technology

A preparatory meeting was held on 18 October to discuss the agenda for the five-day visit by the delegation, led by the three secretaries. A preliminary draft of the discussion agenda was also prepared.

Prothom Alo spoke to at least five members of the delegation about the issues to be discussed with Türkiye. Speaking on condition of anonymity, they said Bangladesh would seek cooperation in areas where Türkiye had made significant progress.

Defence cooperation has been discussed several times at the highest levels between the two countries. Discussions on expanding cooperation in the defence sector are also expected during this visit.

Bangladesh will seek assistance in transferring technology to university students, introducing artificial intelligence (AI) technology in educational institutions and establishing laboratories. The delegation will also discuss training programmes to improve the skills of Bangladeshi government officials.

Officials said discussions were expected on signing a free trade agreement (FTA) and a preferential trade agreement (PTA) between the two countries.

Türkiye has long provided assistance to Rohingya refugees who fled Myanmar and sought shelter in Bangladesh. Disaster Management and Relief Secretary Mohammad Saiful Islam said Bangladesh would seek further Turkish assistance to expand healthcare services in Rohingya camps in Teknaf and Ukhia.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, Saiful Islam said Bangladesh would also seek Turkish assistance to reduce deaths caused by lightning strikes. Türkiye has managed to reduce lightning-related fatalities through the use of technology, he said.

Bangladesh would also seek technological assistance from Türkiye to provide early warnings ahead of earthquakes and landslides, he added.

The disaster management secretary said Bangladesh would seek further assistance for Rohingya refugees as well. Discussions are also expected on establishing an internationally standard hospital and a nursing institute in Dhaka with Turkish funding.

item.title: Gas shortage halts Jamuna Fertilizer Factory again
item.description:
Production at the state-owned Jamuna Fertilizer Company Limited (JFCL) in Sarishabari, Jamalpur, was suspended again on Sunday due to a gas supply shortage, just two days after operations resumed following repairs to a boiler leak.
The shutdown occurred around 5am after Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Limited and Petrobangla stopped supplying gas to the factory.
The plant resumed production at around 10am on Friday after remaining closed for 15 days to repair the boiler leak. However, officials had warned that inadequate gas pressure could force another shutdown.
The factory has faced repeated disruptions over the past two and a half years due to gas shortages and mechanical problems.
JFCL Additional Chief Engineer (Chemical) Md Fazlul Haque said the factory requires 42-43 million cubic feet of gas daily to maintain uninterrupted urea production.
He said production could resume once gas supply was restored, provided the required pressure was maintained.
The factory has a daily urea production capacity of around 1,700 tonnes and can produce 1,400-1,500 tonnes under favourable operating conditions.
Its urea supplies serve 19 districts, including Jamalpur, Sherpur and Tangail. Prolonged shutdowns could disrupt fertiliser supplies, particularly during the upcoming Boro rice cultivation season, increasing dependence on imports and putting farmers under pressure.

item.title: Sakhawat: Govt plans major expansion of cancer care, radiotherapy facilities
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Monday said the government has taken steps to expand cancer treatment facilities across the country, with procurement of new radiotherapy and robotic surgery equipment underway.
“We are working fast to establish eight cancer institutes in the eight divisions and expand radiotherapy services at district level to ensure cancer treatment at the grassroots,” he said.
The minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at the inaugural ceremony of the Medical Physics Program at Brac University in the city’s Merul Badda, Dhaka.
The Mathematics and Physical Sciences Department of Brac University introduced the two-year master's program for the first time in Bangladesh to meet the country’s growing demand for medical physicists.
About the government's commitment to ensure treatment for cancer, Sakhawat said the government has planned to procure 17 linear accelerators to make cancer treatment available across the country.
“We are also going to bring five major robotic surgery machines for the first time,” he said, emphasizing early detection and public awareness as critical components of the government’s cancer-control strategy, particularly for breast and cervical cancers.
He said the government would intensify HPV vaccination campaigns and promote breast cancer self-screening and awareness among women.
“Without awareness, we cannot save people from cancer,” Sakhawat said, urging health professionals and educational institutions to help spread awareness at the grassroots level.
Coming down heavily on the previous ‘fascist regime’, he said the ‘previous fascist government’ had destroyed the country’s health sector, which had been marred by corruption and plundering.
However, after assuming office, the present government has taken robust steps for the development of the country’s health sector, he said, adding that once the projects are implemented, the country would witness a revolutionary change in the health sector within the next two years.
“Under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, we are taking the healthcare services to village level,” the minister said, adding that the government planned to establish Family Wellbeing Centers in every three wards of each union and transform existing community clinics into Health Wellbeing Centers.
“These centers will provide primary-level services, including blood analysis and breast cancer screening,” he said.
Noting that every upazila hospital is going to be transformed into a 150-bed facility, the minister said the government will strengthen dialysis, physiotherapy, and maternal and newborn care at upazila-level hospitals to reduce pressure on tertiary healthcare facilities.
Stating that the government is going to appoint 5,000 doctors soon, Sakhawat said the government is also working to increase the number of hospital beds and recruit around 41,390 health workers, including 25,000 midwives, to strengthen healthcare delivery.
About the newly introduced program at Brac University, he assured government cooperation in developing medical physics education and manpower, saying the government would recruit medical physicists according to the needs of the expanding cancer treatment facilities.
“Medical physics is a very important part of treatment. You do your best and improve yourselves. From the government side, we must extend our hand of cooperation to you,” the minister said.
He said medical physicists play a crucial role in radiotherapy, as the accuracy of radiation dosage is vital for ensuring patient safety and the effectiveness of treatment.
“If the dose is wrong, the patient is gone. If the dose is wrong, the doctor’s credibility is gone,” he said, stressing the need to create adequate numbers of trained medical physicists.
He urged Brac University students, teachers and researchers to contribute to strengthening medical physics and cancer care in Bangladesh.
Professor Emeritus at Dhaka University Dr AFM Yusuf Haider, Additional Director General of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) Professor Dr Jalal Uddin Mohammad Rumi, Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) Clinical Oncology Department Chairman Professor Dr Syed Md Akram Hussain, National Institute of Cancer Research and Hospital (NICRH) Director Professor Dr Mostafa Aziz Sumon and Project Director of Establishment of the Integrated Cancer, Kidney and Heart Treatment Centers across Bangladesh's Eight Divisional Cities Dr Md Toufiq Hasan Firoz spoke as special guests at the event.
Brac University Vice-Chancellor Professor Syed Ferhat Anwar chaired the program, while Mathematics and Physical Sciences (MPS) Department Chairperson Professor Hasibun Naher and Registrar and Controller of Examinations of the university Dr David Dowland delivered the welcome address.
Former Director and Chief Medical Physicist at Gummersbach University Hospital, University of Cologne in Germany, and Adviser and Coordinator of MPS at BRAC University, Professor Dr Golam Abu Zakaria presented the keynote paper, while Medical Physics Program Coordinator Professor Hasin Anupama Azhari presented an overview of the newly introduced program.

item.title: Bangladesh to showcase jute products at COP31 in Turkiye
item.description:
The government plans to showcase Bangladesh’s traditional jute and jute-made products at the UN climate conference COP31 in Turkiye to promote them in international markets.
A special exhibition of Bangladeshi jute products is planned at the Bangladesh pavilion during the conference, scheduled to take place in Antalya from November 9 to 20.
The initiative aims to promote jute as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic and highlight the commercial potential of Bangladesh’s jute industry.
Preparations are underway to display a range of jute products and related technologies at the pavilion. An exhibition display has been set up at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as part of the preparations.
The exhibition will showcase products such as jute bags, home décor items and handicrafts to international buyers, investors and policymakers.
Stakeholders believe growing global awareness of environmental pollution and the need for alternatives to plastic presents an opportunity to expand international markets for jute products.
As a natural, renewable and biodegradable fibre, jute has significant potential in environmentally friendly production and consumption.
At a meeting at the Foreign Ministry on October 15, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam highlighted the potential of Bangladesh’s jute industry during discussions on preparations for COP31 with climate experts and relevant stakeholders. The meeting emphasised promoting jute as an eco-friendly alternative to plastic.
If implemented, the initiative could help showcase the diverse uses of jute, explore new markets and strengthen commercial ties with foreign buyers, while bringing Bangladesh’s traditional “golden fibre” industry into the international spotlight.

item.title: Houthis attack Saudi Arabia before high-stakes talks in Tehran
item.description:
Yemen’s Houthis have kept up their attacks on Saudi Arabia as senior officials from the kingdom, Turkiye and Pakistan are due to hold high-stakes talks with Iran in Tehran on Monday, following warnings of a return to war.
Fresh explosions rattled Riyadh overnight, along with a text message warning to residents, after the Iran-allied Houthis claimed a new attack on the Saudi capital’s international airport on Sunday.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, has become deeply embroiled in the eight-month war since hostilities in its long-running conflict with the Iran-allied Houthis resumed in July.
Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman is among the delegations travelling to Tehran, made up of officials from the three countries that signed a defense alliance in Mecca in August.
Their visit follows warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could resume.
Tensions have increased ahead of Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday and next week’s US mid-terms, where US President Donald Trump’s Republicans are battling to keep control of both chambers of the US Congress.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei will take part in Monday’s meeting with Prince Khalid, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Ali Bagheri Kani, told state TV.
“This historic meeting in Tehran may be the last chance before escalation spirals out of control, an attempt to impose a path of de-escalation before it’s too late,” Hesham Alghannam, a Saudi security analyst and researcher, posted on X.
“The presence of military and security figures at this level together means that the remaining time is extremely limited.”
On Sunday, as blasts rang out over Riyadh and authorities sent texts warning residents of a “hostile aerial threat”, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it struck missile launchers and storage facilities in Yemen.
The Houthis said they had attacked Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport once again. The repeatedly targeted facility has been largely closed since 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in a major attack this month.
Mediation efforts between the US and Iran have been led by Qatar and Pakistan. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Sunday, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.
“Our region is in the grip of serious tensions, and neighboring countries are striving to convey a message and put forward initiatives,” Baqaei said on Monday.
Andreas Krieg of London-based risk consultancy Mena Analytica said Prince Khalid’s presence in Tehran was “hugely significant”, calling him the “strategic mastermind of Saudi Arabia.”
Prince Khalid, brother of Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, has emerged as one of Saudi Arabia’s key diplomatic interlocutors, dispatched on sensitive regional missions.
“For him to go to Iran directly in this very sensitive time is a very, very strong signal that the kingdom is not just... sitting and waiting for things, events to unfold,” Krieg told AFP.
“There’s a clear effort by the Mecca alliance to signal to Iran that they’re ready to work together to defend the kingdom and defend the kingdom’s borders,” he added.
“And so should Iran think to escalate, which they will likely do if Israel and the US strikes, and they will most likely strike Saudi Arabia, Iran will have to bear the consequences.”
Comments by senior officials have raised speculation about renewed hostilities.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday “there has been talk of a new war” but that Tehran’s policies remain unchanged.
Trump said on Friday that Washington “may do another little Epic Fury”, referring to the US-Israeli campaign against Iran that began on February 28.
On Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran may try to disrupt the Israeli elections, where he is in a close-fought race to stay in power.
“We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections,” Netanyahu said.
“Don’t test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows,” added Netanyahu, who has campaigned heavily on his security credentials.
The remarks came as Israel’s Channel 12, citing unnamed sources, reported a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive in the war with Iran, which the premier denied.
